summary: Describes how the standard ANSI IS-IS and ISO ES-IS routing protocols were implemented inside the NSFNET backbone network. It is an implementation description rather than a protocol specification.

plainLanguage.summary: It explains how a big nationwide research network applied a shortest-path routing method to decide where traffic should go.

subtitle: How the NSFNET backbone routed traffic using a shortest-path algorithm.

tldr.problem: A nationwide research network backbone needed an efficient routing protocol to forward traffic between its regional nodes.
tldr.mechanism: The NSFNET backbone used an adapted IS-IS protocol, a link-state protocol based on Dijkstra's shortest-path-first algorithm, to maintain complete network topology and compute optimal routes between sites.
tldr.outcome: The implementation demonstrated how to apply the IS-IS standard to an IP environment with permanent point-to-point connections, serving as a template for backbone networks.

today: RFC 1074 describes how the NSFNET backbone implemented IS-IS routing in the late 1980s. It is not an active standard today but serves as an implementation reference for how IS-IS can be adapted to IP networks with permanent point-to-point connections.

sections.title: The NSFNET Backbone Network
sections.content:
RFC 1074 describes the routing implementation of the NSFNET backbone, a wide-area network that connected thirteen research sites across the continental United States. Each site was linked by permanent point-to-point connections running at T1 speed (1.544 Mbps). The network used specialized switching equipment called Nodal Switching Subsystems (NSS) at each site, which were RISC-based multiprocessor systems running a modified Berkeley Unix kernel.

This document is an implementation description of the ANSI IS-IS and ISO ES-IS routing protocols adapted for the NSFNET environment, rather than a new protocol specification.
sections.plainLanguage: NSFNET was a fast network connecting research centers across America. Each connection point had special switching equipment that routed messages to the right destination.

sections.title: IS-IS Link-State Routing
sections.content:
IS-IS is a link-state routing protocol, meaning each router maintains a complete map of the entire network topology. The protocol uses Dijkstra's Shortest Path First (SPF) algorithm to compute the most efficient routes. IS-IS supports two levels of routing: Level 1 routing handles traffic within an area, while Level 2 routing handles traffic between different areas.

The protocol exchanges information through Protocol Data Units (PDUs). Level 1 Router Link PDUs list neighboring routers, while Level 2 Router Link PDUs list routes between areas. End System PDUs list reachable address prefixes, allowing the protocol to announce external networks.
sections.plainLanguage: IS-IS is like a postal system where each post office knows the full map of the postal network. When mail arrives, it calculates the shortest route to the destination.

sections.title: NSFNET Adaptation and Implementation
sections.content:
The NSFNET backbone implemented a subset of the ANSI IS-IS protocol, supporting only Level 2 routing and permanent point-to-point links. To support IP addresses in the ISO-based IS-IS protocol, the backbone encapsulated IP addresses into Network Service Access Point (NSAP) addresses. Router identifiers used the last four bytes to contain the router's IP address.

IS-IS PDUs were transmitted directly over IP using protocol number 85. The implementation used standard timer parameters: a Hello interval of 10 seconds for keep-alive messages and a hold time of 40 seconds. For inter-backbone routing to regional networks, the backbone used the Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP) and applied policy-based routing filters.
sections.plainLanguage: NSFNET adapted IS-IS to work with the internet by wrapping IP addresses into a special format. Routers sent heartbeat messages every 10 seconds to confirm they were still alive.
